summaries.example: Imagine two groups describing the same moving ball. One group says the ball moves toward its natural place. Another says a force pulls it toward Earth. They use some of the same words, but the words belong to different explanations. Their ideas cannot be matched one sentence at a time, yet we can still compare which explanation helps us solve more problems or make better predictions.
summaries.summary: The word incommensurable means “without a common measure.” In philosophy of science, it describes a difficult relationship between scientific theories that use different concepts, methods, or standards. Thomas Kuhn used the idea to explain scientific revolutions. He argued that a new scientific way of thinking can change the problems scientists work on, the meanings of important terms, and the standards used to judge answers. Paul Feyerabend emphasized that theories can give different meanings to observations, so one theory may not simply be translated into the language of another. Both thinkers were often misunderstood as saying that science is irrational or that different theories cannot be compared. The entry explains that this is not the intended conclusion. Comparison is still possible, although it may involve judgment rather than a simple rule or calculation. The idea challenges the picture of science as a smooth pile of facts that always moves toward one fixed goal. Scientific change can replace older ways of describing the world with new ones.
key_ideas: Scientific theories can use the same words in different ways.
A new theory may change which questions seem important and what counts as a good answer.
Incommensurable does not mean impossible to compare. Scientists can still compare theories by looking at goals such as accuracy, simplicity, and usefulness.
Thomas Kuhn and Paul Feyerabend developed different versions of this idea.
summaries.why_it_matters: This idea helps us understand why major changes in science can be difficult. People may not merely disagree about an answer; they may disagree about the questions, meanings, and standards that shape the discussion. It also encourages care when judging older scientific ideas: we should try to understand them in their own setting instead of forcing today’s meanings onto them.

important_terms.definition: A situation in which two ideas do not have one shared measure or perfect way to match them.
A broad pattern of ideas, questions, and methods that guides a scientific community.
A big change in science that can change its questions, concepts, and standards.
A rule for deciding which things belong together as a kind or group.

questions_to_think_about: Can two people disagree because they use the same word with different meanings?
If a new explanation solves new problems, must it also keep every old question?
How could scientists compare ideas if there is no single perfect rule?
Can a new way of seeing something change what seems like a fact?

summaries.example: Consider the shift from a Ptolemaic model, in which the Sun was classified as a planet moving around Earth, to a Copernican model, in which Earth is a planet moving around the Sun. The word “planet” does not have exactly the same role in the two systems. Kuhn uses cases like this to show taxonomic incommensurability: the theories classify objects through different structures. Still, astronomers can compare their predictions about planetary positions. The theories are therefore not simply incomparable, even though a complete point-by-point translation between them is unavailable.
summaries.summary: Incommensurability originally names the absence of a common measure. Applied to scientific theories, it concerns cases in which rival traditions cannot be compared by translating every statement into a neutral vocabulary and applying fixed rules. Kuhn’s early account treated scientific revolutions holistically. A revolution can alter the problems judged legitimate, the standards for acceptable solutions, and the concepts through which phenomena are understood. His examples suggest that scientists trained in rival paradigms may speak past one another even when they use familiar words. Kuhn later narrowed and clarified the view. Taxonomic incommensurability arises when theories organize objects through incompatible lexical structures. Terms are learned in connected groups, and a change in their relations can make some older claims difficult or impossible to express in the newer lexicon. Methodological incommensurability concerns the absence of a neutral decision procedure: values such as accuracy, simplicity, scope, consistency, and fruitfulness guide theory choice, but scientists may weigh them differently. Feyerabend’s initial account is more restrictive. He applies incommensurability mainly to universal theories whose concepts have different meanings and whose predictions are deductively disjoint. On his view, formal deduction cannot make one rival explain or contradict the other in the straightforward way assumed by some methodologies. Yet Feyerabend uses novel predictions from an alternative theory to support theoretical pluralism and to test entrenched views. Kuhn and Feyerabend differ over the range and strength of the thesis, but both deny that it entails irrationality or total incomparability. Their shared target is a simple picture of science as steady addition,
key_ideas: Kuhn initially described incommensurability holistically, linking changes in problems and standards, concepts, and scientific experience during revolutions.

Kuhn later focused on taxonomic incommensurability and the way theories classify objects through different structures. His no-overlap principle helps explain why a term cannot always be transferred unchanged between theories.
Kuhn distinguished conceptual incompatibility from methodological disagreement. Scientists may share values such as accuracy, simplicity, scope, and fruitfulness while weighting them differently.

Feyerabend described incommensurable theories as deductively disjoint: because key terms vary in meaning, predictions from one theory do not automatically enter formal logical relations with predictions from the other.
Both thinkers rejected the conclusion that incommensurable theories are wholly incomparable or that science is irrational. Comparison can remain rational, though it is not an algorithmic proof.
The entry presents scientific development as non-cumulative in an important sense: revolutionary theories may replace older conceptual structures rather than merely adding facts to them.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate matters because it changes how we understand scientific disagreement and progress. If concepts and observations depend partly on theoretical frameworks, then theory choice cannot always be settled by a neutral checklist. At the same time, rejecting a checklist does not require abandoning rational evaluation. Theories can be judged by their problem-solving ability and by values such as accuracy or fruitfulness, while recognizing that different communities may reach reasonable disagreements.

important_terms.definition: A relation between theories that lack a single common measure because their concepts, classifications, or standards differ.
A scientific framework involving shared problems, concepts, methods, and standards within a community.
Incommensurability produced when theories organize objects into different, partly incompatible systems of kinds.
The view that theory appraisal has no neutral rule that determines one choice for every scientist.
The claim that what counts as an observation is influenced by the theoretical framework used to interpret it.
A system of interrelated terms whose structure makes some statements meaningful within a scientific community.
A view of theory choice in which values guide judgment but do not function as an automatic decision procedure.

questions_to_think_about: Does changing the meaning of a scientific term necessarily change the object being discussed, or can some reference remain stable?
Can shared values such as accuracy and simplicity support rational disagreement rather than eliminate it?
What is gained and lost when historians interpret an older theory using modern vocabulary?
If observations are theory-laden, how can evidence contribute to comparing rival theories?
Does a non-cumulative account of progress require rejecting the idea that science can improve?

summaries.example: Suppose one science club explains why a toy car slows down by saying it is returning to its natural resting place. Another explains the same event using friction and forces. The clubs may agree on what they see but organize it with different concepts. A sentence that makes sense in one explanation may not have the same meaning in the other. Still, they can ask which explanation predicts the car’s motion more accurately or solves more puzzles.
summaries.summary: Incommensurability means lacking a shared measure. The philosophy of science uses the term for relationships between theories that do not fit together through simple translation or one permanent set of rules. Thomas Kuhn connected the idea with scientific revolutions. When a paradigm changes, scientists may change the problems they consider important, the standards they use for acceptable solutions, and the concepts used to describe what they observe. The same word can remain in use while its meaning and range of application shift. Kuhn’s later account focuses on taxonomies, or systems of kinds. A new theory may classify the same objects differently from an older theory, so statements made in one system cannot always be restated without alteration in the other. Kuhn also discussed a methodological form of incommensurability. Scientists may share values such as accuracy, simplicity, scope, consistency, and fruitfulness, but these values do not work like an exact formula. People can weigh them differently and still disagree rationally. Paul Feyerabend developed a related but initially narrower account. He argued that rival universal theories can be deductively disjoint because their key terms have different meanings. As a result, predictions from one theory cannot automatically be used in formal logical relations with predictions from the other. He did not conclude that rival theories could never be tested against one another. Instead, he defended theoretical pluralism: alternative theories can reveal weaknesses in established views and can make new tests possible. Kuhn and Feyerabend differed in how widely they applied the idea, but both challenged the picture of scientific progress as simply adding new facts toward a fixed target. key_ideas: Kuhn argued that scientific revolutions can change more than a list of facts; they can change the problems and standards of a discipline.
A term may keep the same spelling while taking on a different meaning inside a new theory.
Kuhn’s later work emphasized taxonomic incommensurability, where rival theories classify the same objects in different ways.
Feyerabend focused on theories whose main concepts have different meanings, making their predictions deductively disjoint rather than directly linked by logic.
Neither thinker intended incommensurability to mean that theories cannot be compared or that scientists cannot reason.
Theory choice may remain rational even when no fixed method forces every scientist to choose the same theory.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic matters because it shows why scientific disagreements can be deeper than arguments over evidence. Scientists may use different concepts, classify objects differently, or judge theories by different priorities. Understanding this can make us more careful about comparing older and newer science. It also presents a balanced view: scientific reasoning may lack a single automatic method without becoming irrational or impossible.

important_terms.definition: Literally, having no common measure; in science, it describes theories whose concepts or standards do not line up perfectly.
A shared scientific framework that shapes which problems, methods, and answers a community accepts.
A major shift in science that can change its problems, concepts, and standards.
A system for sorting objects into kinds, such as planets, stars, or chemical elements.
The idea that observations are interpreted through the theories scientists use.
A quality used to assess a theory, such as accuracy, simplicity, scope, or fruitfulness.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a new theory make an old scientific question seem unimportant?
Can two theories be compared if they do not use a completely neutral language?
How might the way a person is trained affect what they notice in an experiment?
Should a new theory have to explain every success of the old theory?
Why could reasonable scientists weigh simplicity and accuracy differently?
